title: Tommy John, pioneer of elbow surgery that transformed baseball, dies at 83
dek: Tommy John, the former Major League Baseball pitcher whose name became synonymous with the groundbreaking ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction that revolutionized baseball and extended careers across sports, died on Saturday night at his home in Bradenton, Florida. He was 83.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Tommy John died Saturday night at his home in Bradenton, Florida, at age 83, per NPR reporting.
bottom_line: John's death marks the end of the life of the man whose pioneering surgery saved not only his own career but created a medical and athletic standard that has reshaped baseball and orthopedic sports medicine. His legacy rests not in Hall of Fame enshrinement but in the thousands of athletes who pitch, throw, and play because of what he proved possible.
body: Tommy John died Saturday night at his home in Bradenton, Florida, according to NPR. He was 83. His agent, Mike Maguire, reported the death. John had been in hospice care prior to his death, per NBC News.

John's career in Major League Baseball spanned 26 years and produced 288 wins against 231 losses with a 3.34 earned run average and 2,245 strikeouts, per reporting from NPR and NBC News. He played for six teams: Cleveland, the Chicago White Sox, the Los Angeles Dodgers, the New York Yankees, the California Angels, and the Oakland Athletics. He was a four-time All-Star, according to NPR. John made his debut on September 6, 1963, pitching one inning in relief for Cleveland. He tied for the American League lead with five shutouts in 1966 and led the AL with six in 1967, per NPR. But his career trajectory proved less notable than what came after injury.

On July 17, 1974, while playing for the Dodgers, John tore the ulnar collateral ligament in his pitching elbow. He had a 13-3 record at the time and led the National League in victories going into the All-Star break before the injury occurred against the Montreal Expos, per NPR. He was 31 years old. The injury carried a bleak prognosis: doctors told him his playing career was over.

Dr. Frank Jobe, the Dodgers' team physician, proposed an experimental four-hour surgery on September 25, 1974. Jobe drilled holes in the humerus and ulna bones of John's left arm and inserted a tendon in a figure-eight pattern, replacing the damaged ligament with tissue from elsewhere in his body. Per NBC News, the procedure had never been performed before. Jobe gave it 100-to-1 odds of success, according to NPR. A second procedure rerouted the ulnar nerve, which proved necessary to John's full recovery.

John's arm remained in a cast for four months. By spring training of 1975, he had recovered full range of motion in his left arm, per NPR. The entire 1975 season was spent rebuilding strength. In 1976, John made 31 starts and recorded two shutouts in his comeback year, per NBC News. In 1977, he posted the first of his three 20-win seasons, helping the Dodgers to the National League pennant, according to NBC News. He would go on to pitch for another 14 years after his injury, retiring in 1989 at age 46 with consecutive victories early in that final season, per NBC News. By the time his career ended, John had won 164 games after the surgery, compared to 124 before it, per NPR.

The surgery became known as Tommy John surgery, and its impact proved incalculable. More than 2,600 major leaguers and thousands of amateur athletes have since undergone the procedure, according to NPR. Modern baseball's most celebrated pitchers have had it: Shohei Ohtani, Justin Verlander, Gerrit Cole, and Jacob deGrom, per NBC News. Gerrit Cole, who returned to play for the Yankees in 2026 after the surgery, expressed gratitude to John after the team's August 8 victory, saying, "The surgery itself is saving us, but the player had to step up to the table and do it. Having gone through the process, I can imagine that he was just as diligent, if not more diligent, to the rehab process, and really writing the book for all of us, to a certain extent," per NBC News.

John never won the Cy Young Award. From 1995 through 2009, he appeared on the Hall of Fame ballot but never received more than 31.7% of the votes, falling well short of the 75% required for election, per NPR. He ranked second among pitchers since 1900 with the most wins who were not elected to the Hall of Fame, per NPR.

Born Thomas Edward John Jr. on May 22, 1943, in Terre Haute, Indiana, he was a top baseball and basketball player at Gerstmeyer High, graduating in 1961 as valedictorian, per NPR. He did not deliver the commencement speech due to a stutter, per NPR. Despite being recruited by the University of Kentucky to play basketball, John chose baseball and signed with Cleveland, according to NPR. He was known for his longevity, serving as opening day starter for both the 1966 Chicago White Sox and the 1989 New York Yankees, per NPR.

On August 8, 2026, the New York Yankees released a social media post from John in which he wrote that he wanted to say goodbye to everyone, including friends and fans who had followed him throughout his career, per NPR. He skipped the annual Old-Timers' Day event at Yankee Stadium and issued a statement announcing his retirement from public life, according to NBC News.
John is survived by his wife and three children: Tommy, Travis, and Tamara, per NBC News.

Dodgers President Stan Kasten said in a statement, "Tommy was an exceptional pitcher throughout his career in Major League Baseball, and his courageous role in becoming the first to have surgery that would go on to bear his name can't be overstated. His impact both on and off the field has been felt by ballplayers of all ages and will be for generations to come," per NBC News.

The Yankees released a statement describing John as a "bedrock" of the team's pitching rotation and a favorite among fans, noting that the story of his surgery had overshadowed his work on the mound, which included consecutive 20-win seasons with the club. The team stated, "We pause to remember the totality of his legacy, his competitiveness and skill, his penchant for conversation, his kind and gracious nature, and his stature as an athletic and medical pioneer," per NBC News.

Former Dodgers general manager Ned Colletti posted on X, "Tommy was a wonderful person who competed to the utmost and did what no player had ever done to save his career, in conjunction with the esteemed Dr. Frank Jobe. The HOF is missing Tommy John," per NPR.

Dodgers team physician Dr. Neal ElAttrache told The Associated Press in 2024, "If you put it in dollars and cents, I think there's no question that Tommy John is the most valuable reconstructive procedure there is."
